title: Adaptive slab allocator for KV cache to reduce GPU fragmentation
creator: Sofia Patel
description:
Problem: Continuous batching and multi-tenant concurrent inference workloads produce a highly variable profile of KV cache allocations (different sequence lengths, different model heads and key/value shapes). Our current allocator carves device memory with a single free-list and suffers fragmentation: many small free segments are unusable for hot allocations, leading to unnecessary model evictions, extra kernel launches to copy back/persist KV, and increased latency tail.

Goal: Implement an adaptive slab-style allocator for the KV cache that groups allocations into size classes, minimizes internal fragmentation, and supports low-latency reclamation paths for short-lived entries common under continuous batching. The allocator should: (1) reduce peak device memory usage by at least 12% on typical Llama-variant workloads, (2) lower 99th-percentile token latency regressions caused by KV eviction/copying, and (3) provide telemetry for fragmentation and compaction overhead.

Proposed design summary:
- Size classes: define geometric size classes (powers-of-two-ish) tuned to observed KV sizes (64B, 256B, 1KB, 4KB, 16KB, 64KB).
- Per-stream slab pools: each CUDA stream gets a small per-stream cache of slabs for hot allocations to avoid cross-stream locks. A global arena backs per-stream caches for larger allocations.
- Allocation metadata: keep a compact header per allocation in host-pinned memory (for fast enumerations during compaction) and a 16-bit class tag stored in-device for quick free-path checks.
- Fast free path: free operations place blocks into a per-class free-list. If allocation fits a free block, use O(1) path without taking global locks.
- Background compaction: implement optional background compaction that coalesces small free blocks into larger slabs during off-peak utilization. Compaction runs on a dedicated worker thread that triggers only if fragmentation ratio > threshold (configurable).
- Eviction policy integration: when memory pressure remains, prefer LRU eviction of KV segments within the same size-class to avoid producing many tiny free pieces.
- Alignment & packing: ensure 64B alignment for coalescing and kernel-friendly access patterns.
- Telemetry: expose fragmentation ratio (free bytes / free contiguous biggest chunk), slab utilization per size-class, compaction time per run, and number of allocations serviced from per-stream caches vs global arena.

Trade-offs and constraints:
- Background compaction can interfere with latency-sensitive workloads if run synchronously; therefore, it must be strictly asynchronous and rate-limited.
- Per-stream caches improve latency but increase reserved memory. We need an adaptive cap to avoid wasted allocation on many inactive streams.
- Storing metadata in host-pinned memory adds PCIe roundtrips for some bookkeeping ops; mitigate by caching hot metadata in-device for the hottest N allocations.
- Complexity vs maintainability: this increases allocator complexity and testing surface; we will hide internals behind the runtime allocator API to avoid leaking details into higher layers.

Acceptance criteria:
- Design doc + microbenchmark completeness reviewed by runtime and infra teams.
- Implement allocator with feature-flag (kv_slab_allocator=true).
- Benchmarks: 3 representative workload profiles (short-chat, long-context summarization, multi-tenant mixed) should show >8% reduction in max device memory and lower 95/99 tail RPC latency compared to baseline.
- Telemetry visible in Console: slab utilization heatmap and fragmentation metric queried by route/model.
- Automated unit + integration tests covering alloc/free churn, compaction safety, and multi-stream correctness.

Workplan (high level):
1) Spike (2d): implement a prototype slab allocator in a library build that runs within our runtime process; collect allocation histograms across workloads.
2) Design review (1d): share design doc and telemetry schema (Confluence + dashboard mock).
3) Implementation (7d): production allocator, per-stream caches, free-path optimizations, integration with eviction.
4) Safety & tests (3d): add extensive fuzz tests for fragmentation and race conditions.
5) Pilot (3d): enable flag for canary customers and internal performance suite.
6) Rollout (gradual): enable on runtime-1.24 canary cluster, monitor metrics, and adjust thresholds.

Notes on measurements and success:
- Define fragmentation_ratio = 1 - (largest_contiguous_free_block / total_free_bytes). Aim for <0.45 on mixed workloads.
- Measure extra memcpy / eviction events per 10k requests; aim to reduce by 30%.
- For continuous batching traces, instrument allocation age distribution to tune slab retention time.

Links and artifacts:
- Design doc (Confluence): https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/RT/KV+Slab+Allocator+Design (draft)
- Profiling notebook (Drive): https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1a2b3-example-profiles
- Spike PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/1127

Risks:
- Regression bugs causing silent memory corruption; mitigation: address with aggressive ASAN/UBSAN on debug builds and a staged rollout.
- Lower throughput if global locks are misused; mitigation: lock-free per-class freelists and per-stream caches to keep hot path lockless.

Next steps (immediate):
- Run allocation histogram job across 4-week production traces to confirm size classes (Sofia)
- Prepare design review slides and telemetry schema (Marco)
